map.A ratio: 3 parts mix for every 2 parts w: A ratio: 3 parts mix for every 2 parts water. Order matters.
map.A ratio compares two quantities. 3 : 2 h: A ratio compares two quantities. 3 : 2 here means mix : water. It is part to part.
map.Reader — you're our fifth crew member. M: Reader, you're our fifth crew member. Mix the fuel!
map.Recipe ratio — 3 scoops mix : 2 cups wat: Recipe ratio: 3 scoops mix : 2 cups water. Tap each of the 10 tokens to place it. First tap = MIX. Second tap = WATER. Third tap = back to the bank. Build one batch doubled (the ratio must stay equivalent to 3 : 2).
map.Conceptual: 3 : 2 means for EVERY 3 scoo: Conceptual: 3 : 2 means for EVERY 3 scoops of mix there are 2 cups of water. Doubling a recipe multiplies BOTH numbers by 2.
map.Procedural: 3 × 2 = 6 mix. 2 × 2 = 4 wat: Procedural: 3 × 2 = 6 mix. 2 × 2 = 4 water. Check: 6 + 4 uses all 10 tokens, and 6 : 4 simplifies to 3 : 2.
map.Time trials. Chloe rode 4.8 km in 12 min: Time trials. Chloe rode 4.8 km in 12 minutes. Now Bram is bragging again…
map.Different distances, different times. To: Different distances, different times. To compare fairly we need a unit rate: km per ONE minute.
map.A rate compares two different units (km: A rate compares two different units (km and minutes). A unit rate tells how much per 1. Divide distance by time.
map.Run the numbers, reader. Who's actually: Do the math, reader. Who is really faster?
map.Chloe rode 4.8 km in 12 min. Bram rode 6: Chloe rode 4.8 km in 12 min. Bram rode 6.5 km in 20 min. Find each unit rate in km per minute (divide!). Then pick the faster rider.
map.Conceptual: a unit rate is the distance: Conceptual: a unit rate is the distance in just ONE minute. More distance per minute = faster.
map.Procedural: Chloe: 4.8 ÷ 12. Bram: 6.5 ÷: Procedural: Chloe: 4.8 ÷ 12. Bram: 6.5 ÷ 20. Write each as a decimal. Then compare.
map.Vexhall Library kitchen — 6:00 AM, race: Vexhall Library kitchen. 6:00 AM, race day.
map.Sixty riders registered. Our punch recip: Sixty riders signed up. Our punch recipe makes 5 cups per 12 riders. This is a scaling quest.
map.A ratio table keeps every column equival: A ratio table keeps every column equivalent. Multiply BOTH quantities by the same factor. 12→24 riders means 5→10 cups.
map.Equivalent ratios live in the same table: Equivalent ratios live in the same table. Each column is the recipe, scaled. Never add to just one side.
map.Fill the table before the riders show up: Fill the table before the riders show up thirsty!
map.The punch recipe makes 5 cups per 12 rid: The punch recipe makes 5 cups per 12 riders. Complete the ratio table for race day.
map.Conceptual: every column must be the SAM: Conceptual: every column must be the SAME recipe scaled up. Multiply riders AND cups by the same factor.
Procedural: 12→36 is ×3, so cups = 5×3. 20 cups is 5×4, so riders = 12×4. 12→60 is ×5, so cups = 5×5.
map.I plotted every checkpoint log. A steady: I plotted every checkpoint log. A steady rider makes a straight line through (0, 0)…
map.…but ONE of Torque's points broke the pa: …but ONE of Torque's points broke the pattern. See it glowing red?
map.In a ratio graph, every true point fits: In a ratio graph, every true point fits distance = rate × time. A point off the line is a lie wearing coordinates.
map.Your turn, reader. Find the impostor poi: Your turn, reader. Find the fake point in Torque's log.
map.An honest steady rider at 0.4 km per min: An honest steady rider at 0.4 km per minute makes the line distance = 0.4 × time. Tap the point in Torque's checkpoint log that does NOT fit the pattern.
map.Conceptual: every honest point lines up: Conceptual: every honest point lines up straight through (0,0). The fake point is off that line.
map.Procedural: test each point — multiply i: Procedural: test each point. Multiply its time by 0.4. (5,2): 0.4×5=2 ✓. Keep testing until one fails.
map.Last leg is mine. Juno's report says I r: The last leg is mine. Juno's report says I ride at 0.4 km per minute when I pace right.
map.Ugh — my speed app only speaks miles!: Ugh, my speed app only speaks miles!
map.1 mile ≈ 1.6 kilometers. To convert km →: 1 mile ≈ 1.6 kilometers. To convert km to miles, ask: how many groups of 1.6 fit in 8?
map.Convert the route for my app — fast, Sie: Convert the route for my app. Quick, Sienna is already clipping in!
map.The final leg is 8 km, but Rohan's app s: The final leg is 8 km, but Rohan's app speaks miles. Use 1 mile ≈ 1.6 km. How many miles is the final leg?
map.Conceptual: 1.6 km fits inside every mil: Conceptual: 1.6 km fits inside every mile. So you are asking how many groups of 1.6 are in 8.
map.Procedural: divide 8 ÷ 1.6. (Multiply bo: Procedural: divide 8 ÷ 1.6. (Multiply both by 10 if decimals are hard: 80 ÷ 16.)
map.The handoff zone. 8 km to the finish. To: The handoff zone. 8 km to the finish. Torque's anchor rider is already rolling.
map.Crew analysis complete. Torque's anchor: Crew analysis done. Torque's anchor finishes in 22 minutes. Sienna, can you beat it?
map.Reader — you have my rate, the route, th: Reader, you have my rate, the route, the table, the graph. Make the call!
map.Boss Gate: use everything from this volu: Boss Gate: use everything from this volume. Unit rate, ratio table thinking, and the graph. Make the call.

Torque's anchor finishes in 22 minutes. Sienna rides at 0.4 km per minute and the leg is 8 km (you showed it is 5 miles). Three locks:
map.Final evidence for the judges — which po: Last proof for the judges: which point showed the cheat?
map.Conceptual: time = distance ÷ rate. If y: Conceptual: time = distance ÷ rate. If you know how far she goes in ONE minute, division tells you how many minutes the whole leg takes.
Procedural: Lock 1: 8 ÷ 0.4 (= 80 ÷ 4). Lock 2: compare your answer to 22. Lock 3: which logged point claimed MORE distance than 0.4 × time allows?
